uses: Marshmallow is the classic slippery herb: its root is so full of mucilage that it swells into a soft gel in water. Traditionally the root was steeped in cold water or made into a syrup for a dry, tickly cough and a scratchy throat, and the EMA recognizes it for mouth and throat irritation and for mild stomach discomfort. In folk practice the fresh root or leaves were pounded into poultices for sore, inflamed skin, and the leaves were rubbed on bee and wasp stings. French confectioners once made a soft paste from the root, the ancestor of today's marshmallow sweets, which no longer contain the plant.
energetics: Culpeper called marshmallow moderately hot and drier than other mallows
caution_pregnancy: Safety during pregnancy and breastfeeding has not been established, and the EMA does not recommend marshmallow root then. Not enough is known; avoid.
caution_medications: The thick mucilage may slow the absorption of other medicines taken at the same time, so the EMA advises keeping marshmallow root at least half an hour to an hour away from any other medicine. This effect is described in handbooks but hasn't been confirmed in studies. In mice, marshmallow root mucilage lowered blood sugar, so if you take diabetes medicines, ask your prescriber first and watch for lows. The EMA reports no other interactions.
caution_conditions: See a doctor if a cough comes with shortness of breath, fever or phlegm containing pus, or if symptoms get worse. The EMA does not recommend it for children under 3, or tablets and capsules for children under 6. Don't use it if you are allergic to it. The EMA lists no known side effects.
caution_duration: If a sore throat or cough lasts more than a week, or stomach discomfort more than 2 weeks, see a doctor or qualified practitioner.
caution_topical: None of our sources reports skin reactions to marshmallow poultices. Don't use it if you are allergic to it.
garden_harvest_timing: Grieve picked the leaves in August as the flowers began to open, one at a time, on a fine morning once the dew had dried.
garden_water: Thrives in damp ground and grows larger in moist soil than in dry
notes: A perennial of salt marshes, damp meadows and stream banks, with velvety grey-green leaves and pale pink flowers in late summer. Grieve raised it from spring-sown seed, cuttings, or pieces of root divided in autumn when the stems die back, and said it would grow in any soil. It has been eaten as a vegetable in the Middle East. Grieve traces the name Althaea to a Greek verb about restoring health, and notes that mallows were eaten in times of famine. Culpeper places mallows and marshmallows under Venus.
